analysis.one_liner: Extends the enhanced Affordable Care Act premium subsidies through 2029 and raises the income limit for getting them.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote after being introduced on November 10, 2025, and the enhanced premium subsidies it would have extended are set to lapse at the end of 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Affordable Care Act gives tax credits that lower monthly insurance premiums for people buying coverage on the marketplaces. A temporary, more generous version of those credits expires at the end of 2025. This bill would keep the extra help in place through 2029 and raise the income ceiling for eligibility — from 400% of the federal poverty level to 1000% — so even relatively high-income families could keep getting help with premiums. The bill was sent to the Ways and Means Committee and has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces. If the bill passes, about 20 million enrollees avoid the premium spikes projected when the enhanced credits expire, and households earning between 400% and 1000% of the poverty level become newly eligible for subsidies instead of facing a sudden cliff where their premiums jump to full price.

how_it_helps.text: It extends the enhanced premium tax credits through 2029, keeping monthly marketplace premiums subsidized for households currently receiving them.
It raises the income ceiling for subsidies from 400% of the federal poverty level to 1000%, letting some higher-income families keep help with premiums instead of facing a sudden full-price cliff.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government pays the cost of the larger, longer-lasting credits, which ultimately falls on taxpayers. Insurers would continue receiving subsidized premiums, and the bill does not pay for the extension with new revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the income ceiling for subsidized premiums from 400% of poverty to 1000% of poverty, meaning households well above middle-class income could receive government help with premiums — a costly expansion even relative to simply extending current rules.
The extended and expanded credits have no identified way to pay for them; the added federal cost through 2029 would either increase deficits or need to be offset later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to families facing subsidy cliffs is real and immediate, but the bill extends the most generous part of the subsidies up the income scale rather than phasing it down, and it contains no offsetting revenue, so the full cost falls on federal borrowing. A narrower extension targeted at households below 400% of poverty would have cost less while protecting the people most likely to lose coverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on November 10, 2025, sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and never got a hearing or a vote before year-end, when the enhanced subsidies were set to expire.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Schneider introduced the bill on November 10, 2025, with three Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day; no further action appears in the record.
The bill would extend the enhanced premium tax credits through 2029 and raise the income eligibility cap from 400% to 1000% of the poverty level.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of extending the enhanced subsidies — including members who never brought the bill to a vote — prevailed, and the enhanced subsidies lapsed as scheduled, saving the federal government the cost but raising premiums for subsidized households.

for.name: Rep. Brad Schneider
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend and modify the enhanced premium tax credits.

against.name: Congressional Republicans
against.what_they_did: The House majority did not schedule committee action or floor consideration, letting the enhanced subsidies expire at the end of 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill was referred to a committee controlled by the Republican majority, where it received no action.

industries.note: The ACA marketplace subsidies are paid to insurers as premiums; extending them keeps that federal revenue stream flowing. The bill locks in the insurers' role as the channel through which public healthcare dollars flow.
Fewer uninsured patients means fewer uncompensated-care costs, which hospitals otherwise shift onto paying patients and insurers.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term bill referred to Ways and Means in late November with three cosponsors is very unlikely to advance on its own; the likelier path is that the enhanced-subsidy fight is settled in a larger package or simply allowed to lapse, in which case this bill remains dormant.
